newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr stuck in a rate rut, no end in sight.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr stuck in a rate rut, no end in sight.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept calm atop 75 cents at a thin midsession with traders reporting scant sign of follow-through selling after its offshore pullback.

Indeed, there was little sign of any interest in the currency as the market contemplated further weeks of uncertainty over monetary policy now that the July Reserve Bank board meeting had come and gone with no easing.

Until the policy question was settled one way or the other, traders expected it to hold to this week's US$0.7440/7570 range and were resigned to selling rallies at US$0.7550 and buying dips at US$0.7470 to earn a crust.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the unit was trying to find traction at US$0.7519/24 having slipped from a US$0.7548 high overnight but was only just down on Thursday's late US$0.7530/35 here.

The market's caution was reinforced by persistent rumours an Asian bank was protecting a big strangle option, although traders said this sort of talk often reflected the range bound mentality of the market more than reality.
The impact of the slide in gold prices overnight had been limited so far and analysts reckoned it would remain so unless it threatened to drag the Commodity Research Bureau index down a lot further.
Gold itself is not seen as much of an indicator of inflation any more and has lost much of its relevance to the A$ as a pointer to commodity price trends.

Instead, offshore investors, particularly in the U.S., tend to look at the CRB index as a guide to broad trends in prices. Gold is a part of that and, although only one of 17 commodities covered, did contribute to a 1.85 point drop in the index to 235.57 on Thursday.
The fall was significant since it breached major support around 236.00 and left the index at its lowest level since August 1995.

The index is far fro a perfect match to Australian exports -- it includes such un-Australian products as cocoa, coffee and hog futures and excludes the country's largest export earner; coal. Nevertheless, its influence with U.S. investors meant the break lower would be bearish for the local dollar if sustained.

Dollar bulls had been rather hoping stronger commodity prices would compensate for the currency's dwindling yield attraction in the second half of this year, particularly as it still seemed likely the RBA would cut official rates again.
Many suspected an easing without the promise of commodity support would see the dollar plumb 73 cents.
The next signpost on the policy trail will be employment figures for June next Thursday which should confirm the labour market was flat at best.
A benign reading on inflation and wages later in the month, as analysts expect, would set the scene for another 0.5 point cut in cash rates to 5.0 percent.
On the crosses the dollar was off at 85.57/67 yen from 86.10/20 late Thursday and at 57.3 in trade weighted terms from a previous 57.6 close.
